# Advancing social risk-informed care for people experiencing homelessness

**Authors:** David E. Velasquez; Sahil Sandhu; Katherine A. Koh; Ishani Ganguli

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2Harvard Business School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Harvard Kennedy School of Government, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA | 4Boston Health Care for the Homeless Program, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 5Department of Psychiatry, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 6Division of General Internal Medicine and Primary Care, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## INTRODUCTION

Compared with their housed counterparts, people experiencing homelessness (PEH) are at greater risk of premature death,1 higher healthcare utilization and spending,2 and lower quality of care.3 They tend to describe their care as unaccommodating to their needs and stigmatizing.4,5 Further, hospitalization rates among the PEH population are rising.6 In this context, hospital-based clinicians and care teams must be equipped to deliver patient-centered care to these individuals despite pandemic-induced constraints in hospital capacity.

A 2019 National Academy of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) report offers important guidance for clinicians and care teams caring for this population.7 The report describes health sector activities to integrate social care into healthcare delivery, with the goal of reducing preventable high-acuity care use and improving health outcomes.8 While some activities focus on how health systems should address social needs at the community level, three focus on supporting patients at the clinician level: awareness, adjustment, and assistance (examples are provided in Table 1). From this perspective, we highlight a hypothetical clinical scenario involving challenges that can arise from homelessness that hospital-based clinicians and care teams often face. We then provide examples of how applying clinician-level NASEM activities to PEH may help clinicians and care teams deliver high-quality care to this population.

## THE STATUS QUO: PRE-NASEM FRAMEWORK

Ms. G was a 57-year-old woman experiencing homelessness with a psychotic disorder, substance use disorder, and chronic lower extremity wounds who presented to the emergency department with severe pain and malodorous discharge on her lower extremities. Physical examination, labs, and imaging confirmed dry gangrene on the left lower extremity and wet gangrene on the right lower extremity. She was hospitalized and treated with antibiotics, wound care, and a right below-the-knee amputation. The medical team could not find an appropriate placement for the patient, and she was discharged from the hospital to the streets of downtown Chicago.

Ms. G was re-admitted 1 month later for worsening of her left lower extremity wound that required antibiotic treatment and left tarsometatarsal amputation. During this hospitalization, she expressed difficulties in managing her wound and taking her costly medications while undomiciled. For example, transportation barriers prevented her from filling her tramadol prescription when it was sent to a pharmacy across the city. Ms. G’s primary care team then helped her pick up her medications, but they were promptly stolen by others on the streets. Ms. G’s care team attempted to discharge her to a dual-diagnosis rehab program, but her insurance would not cover this service. She declined a program outside the city that required her to uproot her encampment, belongings, and relationships. Ms. G returned to the streets of Chicago.

## APPLYING THE NASEM FRAMEWORK

### Awareness

Ms. G’s care could have been improved at various points if the NASEM framework had been applied to her care. This process starts with awareness, the first component of the framework defined as “activities that identify the social risks and assets of defined patients and populations.” This routine social risk screening is supported by multiple professional medical societies and is newly included as a quality measure by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) and the Joint Commission for a variety of quality reporting and accreditation programs. To operationalize this approach, care teams must develop strategies to identify PEH and persons at risk for homelessness in their patient populations, which is currently done inconsistently in hospital settings.9,10 Teams can use one of several commonly used, population-specific tools to screen and document their patients’ housing-related risks–such as current or anticipated housing instability and current problems with housing quality (e.g., pests and mold).11 For example, the Accountable Health Communities Screening Tool was designed to help care teams understand if patients did not have a steady place to live (e.g., temporarily staying with others); it is meant to be used in clinical delivery sites, including hospitals, and was recently introduced by the CMS.12 Ms. G could have benefited from the use of this tool or others (see Table 1). Since health systems may not have the capacity to screen for all dimensions of housing-related risks, they might consider prioritizing the questions that make the most contextual sense. For example, resource-rich hospitals that are partnered with community-based housing organizations may include a screening of issues such as housing access and quality, while hospitals with staffing shortages may instead focus on screening for current homelessness to refer patients to nearby homeless shelters at the point of discharge. As demonstrated by Ms. G’s case, understanding patient preferences is crucial to successfully screening and triaging PEH in the most appropriate setting.

PEH often have concomitant social risks, for example, one study found that 77% of respondents experiencing housing instability also experienced food insecurity13–so care teams could administer social risk assessments that include other domains. In one example, PEH who were admitted to Veterans Affairs hospitals were referred to Homeless Patient Aligned Care Teams, who then screened these patients for food insecurity using a single-item validated question.14 The teams followed up positive responses with specific questions related to sources of food, number of meals per day, and diabetes. Ms. G would have screened positive for transportation barriers, perhaps prompting a care team to prioritize prescribing to the closest pharmacy in proximity to where she sleeps or providing her with a public transportation pass.

To operationalize social screening, hospitals can leverage health and social care staff (e.g., case managers and social workers)15 to manually enter reported information into the electronic medical record. Alternatively, patients or caregivers can enter responses on a tablet to feed into their records since electronic self-administered screening may have higher rates of disclosure compared with face-to-face screening.16

### Adjustment

Once care teams identify PEH and their social risks, they can focus on adjustment: altering clinical care to accommodate identified social barriers. For the many PEH with transportation barriers,2 efforts to streamline in-person healthcare contact days may ease the treatment burden. For example, the Veterans Affairs healthcare system provided nearly 1500 video-enabled telehealth tablets to Veterans experiencing homelessness to increase access to care.17 Nearly half of the veterans who received a tablet had a video visit within a month, showing that telehealth may be a viable model in this population. PEH may also benefit from changes in how medications are dispensed upon discharge. So long as standards of care are met, prescribing more pills to minimize pharmacy visits may be beneficial for some PEH, whereas others may prefer shorter prescriptions given the risk of medications being stolen or lost. Additionally, if a patient screens positive for financial insecurity (which is likely for most PEH, including Ms. G) and out-of-pocket cost information is available, clinicians may prescribe a lower-cost medication alternative. Clinicians can normalize these discussions for patients to reduce stigma and improve the chances these approaches succeed.5 One way to do this is by using the PEARR Tool, a trauma-informed, patient-centered framework to discuss sensitive topics that was originally developed for victims of violence.18

Care teams can also adjust clinical care for PEH by finding postacute care placements near the location where PEH spend their days to minimize disruptions. It is not uncommon for patients like Ms. G with transportation-related barriers to decline a postacute care placement outside the confines of their city of residence given the difficulty of returning to the place where they have developed meaningful community relationships. Some clinicians may even be able to adjust care by connecting PEH to street medicine teams to provide longitudinal primary care, as was the case with Ms. G.19

### Assistance

Assistance interventions aim to reduce patients’ social risks by connecting them with social care resources. Low-touch solutions for PEH (which may be preferable for resource-limited hospitals) include providing them with printed resource referral hand-outs of nearby shelter homes and public assistance programs. There are also emerging community resource referral technologies (e.g., WellSky and Unite Us) that tailor resources to patients’ social needs and geography, share referrals with patients via email and text, and track resource connections longitudinally. There is a growing body of research suggesting that PEH have access to, are open to, and may benefit from the use of mobile technologies in health care.17 Other high-touch assistance interventions include referring patients to support staff, such as community health workers, who can connect patients to community-based organizations, government services, or in-house support services (e.g., clinic-based food pantry). Care teams can also refer PEH to housing navigators–when available, as done at Vanderbilt University Medical Center–who can, in turn, link patients with community-based case managers and, if patients qualify and units are available, to supportive housing.10 Hospitals could also consider creating consult teams specifically for PEH to help coordinate the tailoring of services to these patients.

## CONCLUSION

In this perspective, we complement past frameworks20 designed to better care for hospitalized PEH by using examples to illustrate how hospital-based clinicians and care teams can apply the NASEM framework to PEH to help address identified social risks, and ultimately, improve health outcomes. While this is not a systematic review, our aim is to provide examples that might be helpful to healthcare practitioners. Considering patients’ experiences with their social needs provides opportunities to inform clinical care. Clinicians and care teams should continue to enhance care for PEH by following the innovative NASEM framework.
